--- Page 1 ---
AUTOASSUMPTION: SEARCHING OVER ASSUMPTIONS DISCOVERS
ML-SYSTEMS ALGORITHMS
Igor Sadalski 1 Minghao Guo 1 Benjamin Jones 1 Wojciech Matusik 1
ABSTRACT
Many advances in ML systems came from breaking an assumption that earlier methods took for granted: specula-
tive decoding dropped the assumption that a model needs one forward pass per token. Yet algorithms rarely state
their assumptions, so experts and discovery harnesses search over programs, where one edit changes several design
choices and gains are difficult to attribute. Searching over the assumptions themselves remains largely unexplored.
Writing algorithms as proofs makes their assumptions explicit and turns algorithm design into a search over a
small, structured space that an LLM can explore and a proof checker can audit. We formalize 89 algorithms from
KV-cache eviction, weight pruning and speculative decoding as proof graphs with explicit assumptions, checked
in Lean. Our harness, AutoAssumption, relaxes one assumption of a published method, re-derives and re-proves
it, and generates its code. In KV-cache eviction and weight pruning, this search improved on every published
algorithm we ran and produced state-of-the-art algorithms. The eviction algorithm has the highest RULER-4K
score of the published methods we ran, and the pruning algorithm the lowest perplexity of thirteen on four LLaMA
models. At equal budget, the harness scores within a point of OpenEvolve, an open-source implementation of
AlphaEvolve, with a lower standard deviation across repeats. Future work will formalize more fields and combine
them through the principal assumptions they share.

Figure 1. AutoAssumption turns published algorithms into Lean-checked proofs and discovers new ones by changing one assump-
tion at a time. (a) An agent writes each published algorithm as a proof graph of assumptions, definitions and theorems, checked in Lean.
(b) The assumptions of all proofs form one pool. (c) A variant changes one assumption of its parent and re-proves only the statements that
depend on it; Lean rejects a proof that fails (dashed red). (d) Variants that pass are benchmarked, here on RULER-4K and WikiText-2
perplexity, and the scores guide the next change.

1
INTRODUCTION
Many advances in ML systems came from overturning an as-
sumption that earlier methods took for granted. Speculative
decoding (Leviathan et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023) dropped
the assumption that every token needs its own pass of the
arXiv:2611.14844v1  [cs.AI]  10 Nov 2026


--- Page 2 ---
AutoAssumption: Searching over Assumptions Discovers ML-Systems Algorithms
large model, and PagedAttention (Kwon et al., 2023) the
assumption that a request’s KV cache is contiguous. In KV-
cache eviction, five of the seven records after H2O (Zhang
et al., 2023) introduced a new assumption (Figure 2). Each
such advance is easy to explain afterwards but was difficult
to anticipate. We therefore hypothesize that assumptions,
not code, are the productive unit of algorithm design.
Yet both experts and LLM harnesses search over programs,
where it is difficult to tell which assumption produced a gain.
Discovery harnesses such as AlphaEvolve, OpenEvolve and
AIDE (Novikov et al., 2025; Sharma, 2025; Jiang et al.,
2025) and AI-scientist systems (Lu et al., 2024b) edit code,
and a single edit typically touches several design decisions
together. They work on programs because published algo-
rithms seldom spell out their assumptions. A paper often
states an assumption in a single sentence or leaves it in its
code, e.g., whether one KV-cache budget spans all layers,
or when a speculative decoder stops drafting. Experts carry
such assumptions as intuition, which makes it difficult to
change them deliberately.
We propose to make the assumptions explicit by writing
each algorithm as a logical proof. Starting from 89 algo-
rithms with their papers and code, 44 in KV-cache eviction,
26 in speculative decoding and 19 in LLM weight pruning,
an LLM proves that each solves its field’s problem. We
record the proof as a proof graph: its nodes are assump-
tions, definitions and theorems, and its edges are citations
(Figures 3 and 4). A proof counts only if Lean (de Moura
& Ullrich, 2021) checks it completely, with no unproved
statements.
Once we have a proof, we can change one assumption and
derive a new proof and a new algorithm. Changing one
assumption of a proof graph points to the theorems that cite
it, and thus to the parts of the algorithm that must change;
re-deriving them yields a new algorithm with its own proof.
For example, SVIP (Zhang et al., 2025) breaks the fixed
draft length of speculative sampling, and its graph shows
that only the cost claim depends on it. Doing this by hand
is laborious, and these fields publish new algorithms faster
than anyone can re-derive them (Appendix F).
We automate this process with our harness, AutoAssump-
tion, which formalizes published algorithms and changes
their assumptions (Figures 1 and 5). It identifies the problem
a field’s algorithms share, starting from the field’s bench-
mark. It writes each algorithm’s proof graph from its paper
and code, checks it in Lean together with a coverage test
that maps every line of code to a statement of the proof, and
pools the assumptions. It then relaxes one assumption of
a parent, re-derives and re-proves the dependent theorems,
and generates the code before any benchmark run. We ask
two questions about the harness: can it discover new perfor-
mant algorithms, and how does it compare with other LLM
harnesses?
In two fields, AutoAssumption improves on every published
algorithm we ran, and it performs similarly to other har-
nesses. It found a higher-scoring variant for each of the
26 published algorithms it started from. RestoreKV group
mean (ours) (RestoreKV GM) outperforms every published
KV-cache eviction algorithm we ran on RULER-4K, av-
eraged over 2×–64× compression and two models (Fig-
ure 7A). It outperforms its parent by up to 12.0 points at high
compression (Figure 7B). Pruner-Zero layer group (ours)
(Pruner-Zero LG) adds less perplexity over the dense model
than any of the eleven published pruners we tested, at every
sparsity on LLaMA-7B (tied with its parent at 10 %) and
on every model at 50 % (Figure 7E and Table 3, bottom).
SVIP lookup fallback (ours) (SVIP LK) is 4 % faster than
SVIP at batch size 1 (Figure 7G) while keeping its exactness
proof. With the same model and budget, the harness nearly
matches OpenEvolve and scores 0.8 points above AIDE,
and its results vary less across repeats (Section 4.2).
Searching over assumptions thus yields strong algorithms
whose every change is interpretable and checked by proof.
As next steps, we plan to formalize more fields, look for
principal assumptions shared across them and unify the
fields with this method.
Our contributions are:
1. Two new state-of-the-art algorithms for KV-cache
eviction and LLM weight pruning, discovered by our
method. The eviction algorithm scores 75.7 on RULER-
4K, averaged over two models and 2×–64× compres-
sion, against 74.1 for the best published algorithm we
ran. Under the SparseGPT and Wanda protocol, the
pruning algorithm reaches a WikiText-2 perplexity of
6.78 on LLaMA-7B at 50 % sparsity, against 6.89, and
stays best on four LLaMA models (Section 4). A third
variant is a competitive speculative decoder.
2. A blueprint for assumption-based algorithm search,
with performance competitive with code-level har-
nesses. AutoAssumption relaxes one assumption of a
parent, re-derives only what depends on it, and checks
the new proof in Lean before any benchmark run. With
the same model and budget, it scores 0.4 points below
OpenEvolve and 0.8 points above AIDE, with a lower
standard deviation (SD) across repeats (0.75, against
1.39 and 4.09) (Section 4.2, Figure 8).
3. Reformulation of 89 ML-systems algorithms across
three fields. We formalize 89 algorithms as proof graphs
and merge their assumptions into one pool that points
back to every paper.

2
METHOD
We write each algorithm as a proof, change one assumption
at a time and automate both with an LLM harness. Sec-
tion 2.1 writes a published algorithm as a proof graph, a
proof that it solves a formally stated problem with its as-
sumptions explicit. Section 2.2 describes the LLM harness
that automates the formalization and the derivation of vari-
ants over 89 algorithms in three fields (Appendix F).
2.1
Algorithms from three ML-systems fields can be
formalized as proof graphs
We cast every algorithm of a field as a proof graph. A proof
graph is a directed acyclic graph whose nodes are assump-
tions A, definitions D and theorems T , whose edges are
citations, and which ends in the problem statement P. The
assumptions are what the argument takes as given, the defi-
nitions are what the program computes, and the theorems
derive from both that the program solves P. Figure 3 shows
the proof graph of speculative sampling (SpS) (Leviathan
et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023). In SpS, a small drafter Mq
proposes γ tokens and the large target Mp scores them in
one forward pass; an accept-or-resample rule keeps the out-
put distribution exactly that of Mp. Among its assumptions,
the target and the drafter are distributions over the same
finite vocabulary (Assumptions A1 and A2). Among its

(Leviathan et al., 2023) can be represented as a proof graph.
The graph contains every node of Appendix H. Its columns hold
the assumptions A, the definitions D and the theorems T ; open
discs are lemmas L. Each call-out paraphrases the highlighted
node of the same colour, and the badge marks that the proof
compiles in Lean.
definitions is one accept-or-resample step (Definition D3).
From these, it proves that the emitted token has the target’s
distribution (Theorem T1) and derives how many tokens a
step emits in expectation (Theorem T2). Appendix H states
and proves every node.
The problem statement is the algorithm’s contract, and the
theorems prove it. For speculative sampling, the contract
states the output distribution and the number of tokens one
target pass emits. A benchmark measures performance
metrics, such as the speedup on Spec-Bench.

algorithms.
2.2
Variant proofs can be automated with an LLM
harness
Our harness automates the method in three stages (Ap-
pendix A.2). It identifies and formalizes the central problem,
formalizes the existing solutions, and changes the assump-
tions of those solutions to generate variants.
Stage 1: identifying the problem. Stage 1 collects a
field’s reproducible algorithms from its benchmark and
states one problem they all solve. We trace citation net-
works from the core evaluation of a field, i.e., its benchmark
(Appendix A.2.1, Figure 10). We take the papers of the
algorithms that the benchmark already implements, then the
papers that cite them, and a person keeps the algorithms
that are relevant and can run on the benchmark. We rewrite
each kept algorithm in the benchmark as one self-contained
Python file. The file must reproduce the benchmark’s re-
ported scores for an algorithm that the benchmark imple-
ments, and some of the results of the algorithm’s own paper
for an algorithm we ported. An LLM then reads these al-
gorithms and proposes one problem that all of them can
be proved to solve. We keep the problem once a random

Figure 5. A search chain in KV-cache eviction: each accepted
variant changes one assumption of the current best and be-
comes the next parent. The best of the three repeats of Figure 8,
starting from RestoreKV, on a fixed draw of 200 RULER-4K ques-
tions. Above: the proof graphs of variants 1, 4 and 9. The line is
the best variant score so far (RestoreKV itself, 72.9, is not plotted);
filled triangles mark variants that set a new best and became the
next parent, hollow ones variants that did not. Error bars (±1 SD
over question bootstraps, about 0.5; Appendix G.1) barely extend
beyond the markers.
sample of algorithms can be formalized on it, and ask for
a new formulation otherwise. A shared problem makes the
assumptions of different algorithms comparable. For specu-
lative decoding, the benchmark is Spec-Bench (Xia et al.,
2024), and five of our algorithms are decoders it already
implements. We ported 18 more and added 3 baselines, for
26 algorithms in all (Appendix F).
Stage 2: formalizing existing solutions. Two agents turn
each algorithm into a Lean-checked proof, each following
a fixed prompt (prompts in Appendix D, workflow in Ap-
pendix A.2.2 and Figure 11). The first agent receives the
algorithm’s folder, with its code, scores and paper (Ap-
pendix D.1). It confirms by hash that the code is the version
that produced the scores, and writes the proof document
from the code. We treat the code as the source of truth
for what is defined, and use the paper as a guide to which
assumptions to state. The document has one definition per
logic line and ends in a main theorem that the code meets
the problem’s contract. A coverage test checks that the doc-
ument covers every logic line of the code. The second agent
transcribes the document into Lean (Appendix D.2). Its file
states the assumptions, the definitions and the main theorem,
and proves the theorem. A proof counts only if Lean checks
it completely, with no step left unproved. For speculative
decoding, the harness formalized all 26 algorithms. Their
proofs establish exactness for eight published decoders, five
of which had claimed it without proof (Appendix I.1). We
then merge the assumptions of all proofs into one pool.
Stage 3: changing assumptions. We derive variants one


--- Page 5 ---
AutoAssumption: Searching over Assumptions Discovers ML-Systems Algorithms
assumption at a time (workflow in Appendix A.2.3 and Fig-
ure 12). An agent receives a parent’s code, proof and scores,
the pool, and a prompt that describes how to derive a variant
and its proof from the parent’s proof (Appendix D.3). It
makes one move on one assumption, which either relaxes or
strengthens it. A relaxation drops the assumption, weakens
it or replaces it with another algorithm’s answer from the
pool. Ideally, the move comes with a dial, a parameter of
the new assumption whose value recovers the parent. The
agent writes the new assumption and its hypothesis before
any code, and only then derives the definitions and the code
from them. Before any GPU time, the variant must differ
from every known algorithm and from the parent on some
input, and, if it has a dial, reproduce the parent at the dial’s
recovering value. Its proof is the parent’s, edited only within
the impact set of the changed assumption, the statements
that cite it directly or through other statements; the rest of
the proof stays as it is. Changes are marked in red. We then
benchmark the variant in the parent’s setting, and its scores
guide the next choice of parent and assumption. Iterating
from the best algorithm so far gives a search chain. Figure 5
shows one such chain in KV-cache eviction.
3
EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
Our experiments ask two questions:
Q1 Can the harness discover new performant algorithms?
Q2 How does it compare with other LLM harnesses?
For Q1, we run the harness in three fields and score what it
finds against each field’s published methods. The fields are
KV-cache eviction, LLM weight pruning and speculative
decoding, each scored on its own benchmark. Table 1 gives
the main benchmark, model, metric and error bar of each
field; this section adds the other settings, so that others
can reproduce each result. For Q2, we start OpenEvolve,
AIDE and our harness from the same parent algorithm, with
the same model, evaluator and budget, and measure the
best score each finds. Appendix A lists model checkpoints,
software versions and hardware (Table 4), and Appendix G
explains every error bar.
KV-cache eviction. KV-cache eviction is scored on RULER
and LongBench in KVPress, up to 64× compression, with
timing on a dedicated H100. KVPress (NVIDIA, 2024) is
NVIDIA’s eviction library and public leaderboard; it imple-
ments many published algorithms, and we ported the others
to it. RULER (Hsieh et al., 2024) (Table 1) is a synthetic
long-context benchmark of retrieval, variable-tracking, ag-
gregation and question-answering tasks. To test general-
ization, we also use RULER at 8K and 16K tokens and
LongBench (Bai et al., 2024), 3,750 questions from 16 En-
glish tasks with contexts of 2.6K to 30K tokens. Algorithms
evict after prefill, before the question. Most prior work stops
at 16× compression; we extend to the high-compression
regime of 16× to 64×. System metrics are time to first
token (TTFT), including prefill and compression, and the
peak GPU memory that PyTorch allocates. To profile them
reliably, we give each job a whole H100 GPU with no other
load (verified in every run), run it at batch size 1 after an
untimed warm-up, and time it over seven passes.
LLM weight pruning.
Weight pruning follows the
SparseGPT and Wanda protocol on four LLaMA models,
scored by perplexity relative to the dense model. The pro-
tocol is that of SparseGPT (Frantar & Alistarh, 2023) and
Wanda (Sun et al., 2024) (Table 1); beyond LLaMA-7B, we
prune LLaMA-13B and 30B (Touvron et al., 2023a) and
LLaMA-2-7B (Touvron et al., 2023b). Every linear layer
of the decoder is pruned once, without retraining, to 10–
50 % unstructured sparsity, using calibration windows of
2,048 tokens from C4 (Raffel et al., 2020), in fp16 on one
H100 GPU. As in Pruner-Zero’s official code, Pruner-Zero
and Pruner-Zero LG (ours) also take gradient statistics of
the dense model on WikiText-2. WikiText-2 (Merity et al.,
2017) is a language-modeling corpus of Good and Featured
Wikipedia articles; we concatenate its test split (60 articles,
about 245K words), cut it into non-overlapping 2,048-token
windows and take the exponential of the mean per-token
negative log-likelihood. We report this perplexity divided
by the dense model’s, so that 1 means no loss from pruning.
Baselines are eleven published algorithms, re-implemented
from their official code (Appendix A.1), and magnitude
pruning (Han et al., 2015). Each configuration is one run
with a fixed calibration seed.
Speculative decoding. Speculative decoding is scored on
Spec-Bench with two target–drafter pairs, with paired tim-
ing on a dedicated H200. Spec-Bench (Xia et al., 2024)
(Table 1) comes with reference implementations of some
published decoders; we ported the others to it. It spans six
generation tasks, from multi-turn conversation and trans-
lation to mathematical reasoning and retrieval-augmented
generation. Besides the Vicuna pair, we run Llama-3.1-8B-
Instruct as target with Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct (Grattafiori
et al., 2024) as drafter. At T = 0, decoding is greedy and
a correct decoder reproduces the target’s output token for
token; at T > 0, decoding samples with top-k = 50 and a
correct decoder reproduces the target’s output distribution.
Besides the speedup, we report the mean number of accepted
tokens per target pass (#MAT), throughput at T = 0 and
T = 1, and greedy time per output token (TPOT) at batch
sizes 1 to 32. For reliable timing, each run has a whole H200
GPU with no other load, paired runs start minutes apart on
one machine, and each speedup divides by an autoregressive
run of the same target and temperature (Appendix A.1).
Harness comparison.
The harness comparison gives

each search three times and report the mean across repeats
with the minimum and maximum as error bars. Appendix E
describes how we ran OpenEvolve and AIDE.
4
RESULTS
Our harness discovers state-of-the-art algorithms and
matches other LLM harnesses. To answer Q1, whether
the harness discovers new performant algorithms, we ran
it from 26 published algorithms in three fields (11 in KV-
cache eviction, 7 in weight pruning and 8 in speculative
decoding), scored every variant on its field’s search bench-
mark and kept the best one per parent. Every parent has a
variant that scores higher (Figure 6), although the smallest
gains lie within the benchmark noise. Three of these vari-
ants are new algorithms, each one assumption away from
its parent (Table 2): RestoreKV GM and Pruner-Zero LG
outperform every published algorithm we ran in KV-cache
eviction and weight pruning (Figure 7A and D), and SVIP
LK is faster than its parent SVIP at batch size 1 (Figure 7G).
Section 4.1 tests them further against each field’s published
algorithms, on settings the search never saw and in cost. Sec-
tion 4.2 answers Q2, whether the harness performs as well
as other LLM harnesses, by comparing it with OpenEvolve
and AIDE at the same budget; Appendix I adds what the
proofs catch that benchmarks miss.
4.1
Q1: Can the harness discover new performant
algorithms?
AutoAssumption sets the state of the art in two of the three
tested ML-systems fields. In KV-cache eviction, RestoreKV
GM (ours) scores 75.7 on RULER-4K, averaged over both
models and six compression ratios, against 74.1 for KVGrad,
the best published algorithm we ran (Figure 7A). It leads
on each model separately (77.0 against 75.4 on Llama, 74.5
against 72.9 on Qwen; Appendix Table 5). The strong algo-
rithms all stay near 95 at 2×–8×; the lead comes at 16× and
32×, up to 12.0 points over its parent (Figure 7B). In weight
pruning, Pruner-Zero LG (ours) has the lowest perplexity of
thirteen pruning algorithms we ran: on LLaMA-7B at 50 %
sparsity it reaches 1.195 times the dense model’s, against

does this performance generalize beyond the search setting?
The two best discovered variants generalize beyond the
search setting. In KV-cache eviction, the search scored
RestoreKV GM on 200 RULER-4K questions. On all 6,500
questions it improves its parent by 3.1 points on Llama-3.1-
8B-Instruct and by 2.4 points on Qwen3-8B. The gain holds
at longer contexts, by 3.1 and 3.3 points at 8K and 16K
tokens, and on another dataset, by 1.5 points on LongBench
(Bai et al., 2024) (Table 3, top). In LLM weight pruning,
the search scored Pruner-Zero LG on LLaMA-7B at 50 %
sparsity. It has the lowest perplexity of all thirteen pruning
algorithms on LLaMA-7B, 13B and 30B, and on average
adds 10 % less perplexity above the dense model than its
parent, the best published pruner. It is also best on a different

The best variants remain practical, at costs close to their par-
ents’. For each parent–variant pair we test the ratio of the
variant’s cost to its parent’s for a difference. The time to first
token of RestoreKV GM (ours) is 1.03 times RestoreKV’s,
pooled over contexts from 4K to 64K tokens, and not sig-
nificantly different from it (p = 0.69; Figure 7C; Appendix
Table 8). At 4K tokens on both models the difference is
also not significant (p = 0.39), and its peak GPU memory
is identical to its parent’s. SVIP LK (ours) stays within 4%
of SVIP’s time per output token at every batch size up to
16 (Figure 7I); paired over questions and pooled over these
batch sizes, it is 2.3% faster (90% CI 2.0–2.6%). At batch
size 32, however, it is 11.7% slower (90% CI 10.6–12.7%).
Pruner-Zero LG (ours) prunes LLaMA-7B in 48 s against
53 s for its parent (Figure 7F).
4.2
Q2: How does the harness compare with other
LLM harnesses?
Searching over assumptions improves more consistently
than searching over code. We compare with two code-level
harnesses: OpenEvolve (Sharma, 2025), an open-source
implementation of the prominent AlphaEvolve (Novikov
et al., 2025), and AIDE (Jiang et al., 2025), a widely used
tree search over programs. All three start from RestoreKV
with the same model, evaluator and budget. The code-level
harnesses gain most in their first steps: after two algorithms,
OpenEvolve and AIDE reach 76.1 and 75.4 RULER points,

Figure 8. AutoAssumption finishes level with the code-level
LLM harnesses and improves more steadily, with a smaller
spread across repeats. OpenEvolve and AIDE jump early and
then gain little; AutoAssumption, changing one assumption per
step, rises at almost every step and ends at 79.3, against 79.7 and
78.5. All three start from RestoreKV; Fable from scratch has no
parent. Scores average 200 RULER-4K questions, Llama-3.1-8B-
Instruct and Qwen3-8B, and 2×–64× compression. Lines: mean
of three repeats; error bars: minimum to maximum.
against 70.7 for ours. We hypothesize that each of their
edits changes several design choices at once, which allows
a large early jump but gives little guidance for the next
change; over the remaining eight algorithms they add only
3.6 and 3.1 points. Our harness changes one assumption
per step and keeps rising, by 8.6 points over the same steps.
After ten algorithms it reaches 79.3 points, against 79.7 for
OpenEvolve and 78.5 for AIDE, while Fable from scratch
converges lowest, at 71.4 (Figure 8, Table 12). Searching
over assumptions thus matches searching over programs,
with every change attributable to one assumption and a
smaller spread across repeats (1.3 points after ten algorithms,
against 2.5 and 7.1).
5
RELATED WORK
Axiomatic design. The Axiomatic Atlas (Guo & Matusik,
2026) audits architectures against one fixed axiom set; we
recover each algorithm’s own assumptions. The Atlas states
the requirements on a neural architecture as composable
axioms over connectivity, operator contracts, depth stabil-
ity and merges, and an audit returns a certificate or names
the violated axiom, which implies a targeted repair. Our
assumptions come from a Lean-checked proof of each algo-
rithm, and a changed assumption dictates the re-proof and
the code that the benchmark then scores.
Automated design search. Code-level harnesses evolve
programs against a fixed evaluator (Romera-Paredes et al.,
2024; Novikov et al., 2025; Sharma, 2025; Lange et al.,
2026; Jiang et al., 2025), also for ML research (Lu et al.,
2024a; Hu et al., 2025a; Lu et al., 2024b), systems research
(Cheng et al., 2025b;a) and KV-cache eviction (Poudel et al.,
2026; Yu & Chai, 2025; Park & Hwang, 2026). Their gains
are difficult to attribute, and simple baselines often match


--- Page 9 ---
AutoAssumption: Searching over Assumptions Discovers ML-Systems Algorithms
them (Gideoni et al., 2026; Oved et al., 2026). Our harness
instead changes one stated assumption per step.
Assumptions and formal verification. Tracked assump-
tions go back to truth maintenance (de Kleer, 1986) and
structured proofs (Lamport, 2012) and underlie formal
blueprints (Massot, 2021; Pacalet et al., 2009). Assump-
tionMiner makes the assumptions behind LLM-generated
code explicit (Wu, 2026); SampCert, AutoOPT, LegoNE,
LLMLift and Algorithmist derive algorithms together with
proofs (de Medeiros et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2026; Li et al.,
2026; Bhatia et al., 2024; Kulkarni, 2026); and ProofLoom
formalizes published algorithms in Lean (Wang et al., 2026).
These works handle one algorithm at a time; we pool as-
sumptions across a field and, as in proof repair (Ringer et al.,
2019), re-prove only what a change affects.
6
LIMITATIONS
Three limitations remain: human review, fields that resist
formalization and non-canonical assumptions. First, the for-
malization needs a human reader. Lean checks each proof
against the problem statement, not the statement against the
field, so a person must confirm that the contract says what
the field means. Second, a proof covers only what mathe-
matics can represent. In ML systems, a proof can show that
an eviction algorithm uses less memory or that a decoder
samples the target’s distribution exactly. Training dynamics,
or the quality of an LLM’s answers, depend on statistics of
the data that we do not fully understand, so we cannot build
a proof around them; only the benchmark measures them.
Third, the assumptions are not canonical. The LLM chooses
how to split an algorithm into assumptions, and some of
them, such as how the GPU is structured, admit several lev-
els of detail or stay implicit. A second formalization could
state a different set that still proves the contract and suggests
different variants. We have not measured how stable the
pool is across repeated formalizations.
7
CONCLUSION
ML-systems algorithms have advanced by breaking assump-
tions, yet these usually stay implicit. Writing algorithms as
proofs makes them explicit and turns algorithm design into
a search over a small, structured space that an LLM can ex-
plore and a proof checker can audit. In two fields, KV-cache
eviction and weight pruning, this search improved on every
published algorithm we ran and produced state-of-the-art
algorithms. Our results support the view that assumptions,
not code, are the productive unit of algorithm design: they
make each change interpretable, its effect attributable and its
correctness checkable. As future work, we plan to formalize
more fields and improve their algorithms. We then plan to
look for principal assumptions shared across fields and to
combine the fields. Together, these steps would formalize
the discipline as a whole.

AI USAGE DISCLOSURE
Under the authors’ direction, Claude Code (Anthropic) was
used for experiment code, scheduling and evaluation scripts,
figure and table scripts, and manuscript assistance. Ope-
nAI Codex assisted this revision by auditing consistency,
checking existing numerical artifacts, generating a matched
comparison figure and editing the manuscript. The authors
are responsible for reviewing the final text, code, citations
and claims. LLM-generated algorithms, proof documents
and code studied as experimental outputs are identified as
such in the paper.

A
REPRODUCIBILITY
This appendix gives what is needed to rerun our experiments. Appendix A.1 lists the benchmarks, models and machines of
the three fields, and Appendix A.2 gives the steps by which our harness produces a design proof and a variant.
A.1
Reproducing external results
Each field ran on its own machine (Table 4), one job per whole GPU through a shared queue. Every score records its
machine, software versions, run date and the SHA-256 of its code, and each algorithm is released with its proof, code and
scores. Checkpoints and datasets come from the Hugging Face Hub (Spec-Bench from GitHub) at the revisions recorded
with the results; Appendix E pins OpenEvolve and AIDE.
Table 4. GPU, NVIDIA driver, CPU, Python, PyTorch, libraries and precision of the machine behind each field’s experiments
(KV-cache eviction, weight pruning, speculative decoding). One GPU per job. Driver column: highest CUDA version the driver
supports; brackets: CUDA runtime PyTorch was built against.

KV-cache eviction.
Every algorithm runs as a press of KVPress (NVIDIA, 2024) 0.5.5 on one H100, evict-
ing after prefill and before the question at compression ratios from 2× to 64×.
The models are Llama-3.1-8B-
Instruct (NousResearch/Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, with Meta’s Llama-3.1 chat template) and Qwen3-8B
(Qwen/Qwen3-8B), in BF16. RULER (Hsieh et al., 2024) (simonjegou/ruler) has 13 synthetic tasks at 4,096 tokens,
500 questions each, scored by the mean per-task accuracy. The searches used a nested 200-question subset (seed 42), so the
6,500-question scores of Table 6 are not held out.
The other KV-cache settings ran on two other machines. RULER at 8K and 16K tokens and the 16 English tasks of
LongBench (Bai et al., 2024) (Xnhyacinth/LongBench, 3,750 questions) in Table 3 (top) ran on a second H100
machine (NVIDIA driver 580.178.04, CUDA 13.0, Intel Xeon Platinum 8481C, PyTorch 2.14.1+cu130, otherwise as the
first row of Table 4). The 300-question scores of the prior algorithms in Figures 2 and 13 ran on the H200 machine with the
KV-cache software (PyTorch 2.14.1+cu130). Our re-runs, the parent rows of Tables 6 and 3, agree with NVIDIA’s KVPress
leaderboard within 0.4 RULER points across all 41 points (Figure 9a).
Weight pruning.
Pruning follows the protocol of SparseGPT and Wanda on LLaMA-7B, 13B and 30B
(huggyllama/llama-7b, -13b, -30b) and LLaMA-2-7B (NousResearch/Llama-2-7b-hf) in FP16. Every
linear layer of the decoder is pruned once, layer by layer, without retraining. Calibration draws 128 random 2,048-
token windows (seed 0) from the first C4 training shard (allenai/c4, en/c4-train.00000-of-01024); Pruner-
Zero computes its gradient statistics of the dense model on WikiText-2. The scores are WikiText-2 test perplexity
(wikitext-2-raw-v1, 2,048-token windows) and, at 50 %, the mean zero-shot accuracy of lm-eval 0.4.13 on Wanda’s
seven tasks (BoolQ, RTE, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, ARC-easy, ARC-challenge, OpenBookQA).
The eleven published algorithms are single files ported from their official code, run in one harness on the KV-cache H100
machine (78 runs on the second H100 machine). Where their papers report a cell, our perplexities agree within 0.1. Each
cell is one run; its error bar is a bootstrap SE over the 166 WikiText-2 windows.
Speculative decoding.
Spec-Bench (Xia et al., 2024) (hemingkx/Spec-Bench, commit fd2c1cd) has 480
questions in six tasks.
The target–drafter pairs are Vicuna-7B-v1.3 (lmsys/vicuna-7b-v1.3) with vicuna-


--- Page 19 ---
AutoAssumption: Searching over Assumptions Discovers ML-Systems Algorithms
68m (double7/vicuna-68m) and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (NousResearch/Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct)
with Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct (unsloth/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct);
the two Llama models share Meta’s
Llama-3.1 chat template and tokenizer.
The native baselines use Spec-Bench’s code with the Medusa
(FasterDecoding/medusa-vicuna-7b-v1.3), EAGLE (yuhuili/EAGLE-Vicuna-7B-v1.3) and Hydra
(ankner/hydra-vicuna-7b-v1.3) heads; SVIP follows its authors’ code (Geralt-Targaryen/SVIP, commit
0cd912e). Every algorithm runs in Spec-Bench’s unmodified evaluation loop, which does the prompting, warm-up and
timing, on all 480 questions, with at most 1,024 new tokens, in FP16 under Transformers 4.37.1.
SVIP keeps its authors’ constants (stop drafting when
√
cH > h with c = 0.15, h = 0.3; at most 40 draft tokens), and SVIP
LK (ours) adds only PLD’s prompt-lookup parameters (suffix n-grams up to 3, at most 10 lookup tokens). At T > 0, drafter
and target sample with the same temperature and top-k = 50. Each #MAT and speedup cell, at five temperatures, is the
mean of three paired runs with seed 0, so the runs of an algorithm emit the same tokens and differ only in timing.
Timed runs are isolated and paired. Each is its own queue job on a whole H200, whose only other context is an idle
placement anchor that launches no kernels; no two of the 60 SVIP and SVIP LK (ours) runs shared a GPU. Run k of SVIP
and of SVIP LK (ours), for the same model pair and temperature, started within 15 minutes of each other (median 3) on two
GPUs of one machine, and each speedup divides by the autoregressive run k of the same target and temperature.
The systems profiles behind panels G and I of Figure 7 ran on the H200 machine after a driver update (615.71.10, CUDA
13.4). Each job times the algorithm and an autoregressive pass of the same target on the same GPU and inputs, synchronising
CUDA at phase boundaries after three untimed warm-ups; timings exclude loading, tokenization and warm-up. Our
Spec-Bench re-runs agree with its leaderboard within 0.2 accepted tokens per target pass (Figure 9b).

A.2
Reproducing our harness
The harness has three steps, each on its own page with a diagram: preparing the shared problem formulation (Appendix A.2.1)
and formalizing a published algorithm (Appendix A.2.2), which run once per field as the offline stage of Section 2.2, and


--- Page 20 ---
AutoAssumption: Searching over Assumptions Discovers ML-Systems Algorithms
making variants (Appendix A.2.3), the online stage. In each step an agent follows a prompt of Appendix D: Prompt 1 writes
an algorithm’s proof document from its code, Prompt 2 transcribes it into Lean, and Prompt 3 derives a variant and its proof.
The harness also needs the benchmark, a Lean 4 project with Mathlib, an agent that reads and writes files and runs scripts,
and GPUs.


--- Page 21 ---
AutoAssumption: Searching over Assumptions Discovers ML-Systems Algorithms
A.2.1
Preparing the shared problem formulation
Start from the field’s benchmark (Figure 10a). Take the algorithms it implements and the papers that cite them, and let
a person keep those that are relevant and can run on the benchmark. Rewrite each as a self-contained code.py that
reproduces the benchmark’s reported scores or, for a ported algorithm, some of the results of its own paper. Ask an LLM
harness for one problem that every algorithm could be proved to solve (Figure 10b), and formalize a random sample of
algorithms on it (Appendix A.2.2). Keep the problem and formalize every algorithm on it if a Lean file builds for each of
them; otherwise, ask for a new formulation.

A.2.2
Formalizing a published algorithm
Two agents formalize each algorithm in turn (Figure 11). The first, with Prompt 1, writes the proof document from the
algorithm’s code, not its paper: every definition transcribes a line of the code, up to a main theorem that the code meets
the shared problem’s contract. The second, with Prompt 2, reads proof.tex and code.py and writes axioms.lean,
with the assumptions and the main theorem’s statement, and proof.lean, which adds the proofs. Last, we group the
assumptions of all algorithms by the design question they answer into one shared pool.

A.2.3
Making variants
One agent makes each variant in a copy of the parent’s folder (Figure 12). Following Prompt 3, it reads the parent’s
code.py, proof.tex and scores and the shared pool, chooses one move on one assumption, often borrowed from the
pool, and writes the new assumption and its hypothesis before the smallest code change. Before any GPU time, the variant
must be no known algorithm, reproduce the parent at one parameter value and differ from it on some input. Its proof edits the
parent’s only within the impact set of the changed assumption (changes in red, borrowed text in yellow). We benchmark it in
the parent’s setting, compare it with the literature and verify it; its scores guide the choice of the next parent and assumption.

Open the assumption catalog; per class, compare
the parent’s choice with other algorithms’ alterna-
tives. Choose one perturbation: borrow, combine,
relax, augment, drop, add, or your own.
Create the variant’s workspace with copies of the
parent’s code and proof; edit only the copies.
Before any code: the perturbed assumption, the
hypothesis, the guarantees lost or gained; source
method and label of anything borrowed.
Derive the new definitions; implement them with
the smallest diff to the parent’s code; record hash
and diff.
Duplicate check against every known method:
assumptions, pseudocode, and outputs on a few
inputs if one could be identical.
Before the GPU: reduction, variant(𝜃0) repro-
duces the parent’s output; non-equivalence, the
outputs differ.
1
2
3
4
5
6
7
Match: change the
perturbation.
Fails: fix the code.
Prove, run and check (steps 8–13)
Impact set on the parent’s original proof; apply
the red and yellow edits in document order; only
the impact set may turn red.
Re-read the variant’s code top to bottom against
the finished document.
Build with no warnings; look at every page. Diff
against the parent: every difference inside \Old,
\New, \Borrowed.
Run in the parent’s evaluation setting; report the
change per setting.
Literature review: papers, preprints, code with the
same assumptions or algorithm; cite the closest,
say how the variant differs.
Verification: submit code, proof and review; fix
every error.
Variant: code, proof (changes red, borrowed yel-
low), review, scores. It joins the pool of algo-
rithms that later variants start from.
8
9
10
11
12
13
Outside: fix the
edits.
Scores to the
agent: next par-
ent (step 1).
Published match:
change the pertur-
bation (step 2).
Resubmit, ≤5
rounds; report
what stays open.

the agent; red: checks and the step a failure returns to, as in Figure 11.

Figure 13. KVGrad EA (ours) lies above every prior design at 16×–64× compression, where it gains 6.9 points on average over
its parent KVGrad (3.7 points over 2×–64×). RULER-4K, mean of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen3-8B. The 33 query-agnostic
prior designs (grey unless the legend names them) are each drawn at the largest number of questions both models finished (300 or 6,500);
KVGrad EA (ours) and KVGrad use 6,500. Table 5 lists the named prior algorithms per model.
We ran 34 published KV-cache eviction algorithms on all twelve RULER-4K cells; RestoreKV GM (ours) (75.7) has a
higher mean than every one of them, the best being KVGrad (74.1). Table 5 lists the published algorithms Figure 13 names,
with RestoreKV GM (ours), which has the best mean among them. It holds the best score in four of the six 16×–64×
cells; KVGrad keeps 64× on Llama (26.0 against 25.2) and 32× on Qwen (54.9 against 54.0). At 2×–8× the published
algorithms are as good. Three algorithms drawn only in grey would change a mark: CaM (TOVA) (38.4) and NestedKV
(33.8) at 64× on Llama, and DefensiveKV (Feng et al., 2026) (96.0) at 2× on Llama, all at 300 questions.

B.1.3
Systems cost
Table 8 gives the time to first token of no eviction, four published algorithms and RestoreKV GM (ours) across context
lengths; Figure 7C plots these times, and Section 4.1 tests it. RestoreKV GM stays within the run-to-run spread of RestoreKV
at every context. KVGrad is the slowest by far: its compression takes 3 to 14 min at 32K and 64K.

B.2
Speculative decoding
The bars of Figure 7G are the published decoders Hydra (Ankner et al., 2024), EAGLE-2 (Li et al., 2024b), Medusa
(Cai et al., 2024), MCSD (Yang et al., 2024), acceptance feedback (Gante, 2023), SVIP (Zhang et al., 2025), confidence
stopping (Mamou et al., 2024b;a), AdaEDL (Agrawal et al., 2024), speculative sampling with fixed K = 5 (Leviathan et al.,
2023; Chen et al., 2023) and PLD (Saxena, 2023). SVIP LK (ours) adds a prompt-lookup fallback to SVIP (Algorithm 3).
Figure 7G uses the systems-profile runs (Appendix A.1).
B.3
LLM weight pruning
Pruner-Zero LG (ours) is the best pruner in every perplexity column, and its lead grows with sparsity. Tables 9 and 10
give the cells behind panels D and E of Figure 7 and the bottom of Table 3. The margin over the second best grows from
below 0.01 at 10 % to 0.10 at 40 % and 0.11 at 50 %. On the zero-shot tasks (Table 11) no pruner is best on every task;
Pruner-Zero LG (ours) gains on its parent on three of the seven tasks and on the mean (+0.3). Each cell is one run with a
fixed calibration seed (Section 3); the LLaMA-30B cells of ALPS, GBLM-Pruner, Pruner-Zero and Pruner-Zero LG (ours)
ran on the first H100 machine and the other LLaMA-30B cells on a second one (Appendix A.1).

AutoAssumption: Searching over Assumptions Discovers ML-Systems Algorithms
D
PROMPTS FOR MODELS
The model works from three prompts, one per step, each printed on its own page. We give them here in a setup-independent
form: we leave out file layout, tooling and algorithm-specific examples, so the prompts apply to any algorithm with a stated
specification and can be adapted to another code base. The prompts are printed as plain text: their instructions on the
typesetting of the documents are left out.
Each prompt covers one step of the method. Appendix D.1 writes the proof document of an algorithm, built mainly on
its benchmarked code (Section 2.2). Appendix D.2 writes the Lean proof from a finished proof document. Appendix D.3
derives a variant from a parent’s proof by changing its assumptions, with every change marked and every borrowed statement
attributed. Figures 11 and 12 (Appendix A.2) show where each prompt is called and the workflow it sets out.


--- Page 34 ---
AutoAssumption: Searching over Assumptions Discovers ML-Systems Algorithms
D.1
Designing proof files
Prompt 1: writing the proof document of a design
How to write a proof document: the code of one design as mathematics
A proof document takes one design (a method with its paper and the code that was benchmarked) and produces an
exact mathematical description of that code, as it actually ran, stated only as assumptions, definitions, lemmas,
theorems and proofs, ending in a theorem that running this code meets the design’s specification: the one property
the design is required to guarantee. That property is the only claim proved. Nothing about optimality, nothing about
quality, nothing beyond it. The finished document is later formalized in Lean, following its proof structure.
The point of the whole exercise. The benchmarked code is the code for which we have performance numbers. The
document is about that code: it shows that this code, when run, provably meets its specification, the way verified
software is shown to meet a specification. Therefore the single most important requirement is that the document
represents the code exactly, so that every definition is a faithful transcription of a line of the code that runs, and every
design decision the code makes is explicit in the document. If the description is exact, a Lean proof about the
description is a proof about the code. If it is not, the Lean proof certifies nothing. Everything else in this guide serves
that requirement.
Inputs and outputs
Inputs, gathered for the design before a proof is started:
−the benchmarked code, with a hash identifying the exact version that ran;
−the paper;
−the authors’ original paper source and original code, when available, with a record of where they came from (if
either is missing, record that; do not pretend).
Outputs, stored with the design’s other inputs:
−the proof document, structured as described under the heading on the proof document in order;
−a provenance record: the version of this guide the proof follows, the hashes of the proof document and of the code
it was written against.
The proof is built mainly on the benchmarked code
The proof is built mainly on the benchmarked code. It is the code that produced the results; it is the ground source.
Every assumption, definition, lemma and theorem of the document is about it. Before starting, confirm that the code
at hand is the version that ran (its hash must match the version that produced the results). If it does not, stop and
resolve that first; a proof about a different version is worthless.
The proof can also look at the paper and at the authors’ reference code, to understand the benchmarked code:
−The authors’ original code shows what a line of the benchmarked code is a port of and what an ambiguous line
intends. Nothing from it enters the document unless the benchmarked code does the same thing, and then the
document describes the benchmarked code.
−The paper and its source matter for one specific thing: assumptions. The paper motivates the method’s steps and
states the assumptions under which they are meant to work. Read it to understand the motivation of a part of the
code and to find assumptions relevant to it (what is taken to be given, what is taken to be negligible, what a step
presumes about its input). Such an assumption, when the code indeed relies on it, is written in the document as an
assumption in the document’s own words. Nothing is quoted from the paper, and no definition or theorem is written
from the paper: the paper may tell you what to assume, the code tells you what is defined.
What is proved
For each design, one statement: running the benchmarked code on any input that satisfies the stated assumptions
produces an output with the property the specification requires.
The specification is fixed by the problem the design solves, not by the design. State it precisely: what the input is,


--- Page 35 ---
AutoAssumption: Searching over Assumptions Discovers ML-Systems Algorithms
what the output is, the quantity or relation the claim is about, and the exact form of the claim (an equality, an
inequality, a containment, an identity of distributions). Where the design’s output determines an exact amount (how
much is saved, how many items are kept), prove the exact amount, not only its direction.
The problem statement is written so that the specification is the natural thing to prove: the problem states what must
be achieved, the code is a procedure, and the theorem says the procedure achieves it. If the claim depends on how
the output is stored or used, state that as an explicit assumption; without it the claim may not hold, and the document
must say so in that assumption.
The proof document, in order
Everything in the document is one of: assumption, definition, lemma, theorem, proof. There are no explanatory
paragraphs and no prose that describes the design in words, because such prose is not a statement that can be
checked. What belongs is a definition as a formula, an assumption stating what is taken as given, and a theorem
stating what follows. Every statement must be one that Lean could verify: it has a precise form (a formula, a set, a
function, an inequality, an equality, a count), it names the assumptions it uses, and if it is a lemma or theorem it has a
proof. Where a reader would need a word of explanation, put it inside the statement being explained (a definition’s
label, a remark line inside a definition saying which part of the code it transcribes), not in a paragraph between
statements.
Symbols
First, list every symbol that appears in the definitions and in the theorems: shapes and sizes, inputs, parameters,
intermediate objects, the quantity the specification is about. For each symbol give its meaning and where it is defined.
Problem statement
State what the input is, what the output is, the quantity or relation the specification is about, and the claim to be
proved. Immediately after the problem statement: the assumptions the problem statement itself needs so that its
objects exist, each a formal statement with quantifiers written out, and one lemma that the problem is well posed. All
other assumptions are introduced at the section of the code that first needs them.
Where the problem definition comes from. If several designs should share one problem definition, the user provides it;
use it as given, for every one of those designs. Otherwise, come up with the simplest problem definition that can be
verified: the smallest input, output and claim that the code’s behaviour can be checked against.
Reading the code exactly
Always, before writing a line of the proof, read the code itself. The document transcribes it directly. Every definition
must follow the code:
−in the order the code runs, with the same indexing (say which convention is used and convert consistently), the
same rounding, the same tie behaviour and the same boundary cases;
−covering every branch of the code that can run in the benchmark, including flags fixed to a constant. A branch that
cannot run is handled by an assumption stating the setting that excludes it, as described under the heading on
sections of the code;
−without programming−language constructs. Every library call, array operation or sentinel value becomes
mathematics: a set−builder, a sum with its indices written out, a maximum over an explicit set, a selection with its tie−
break, a slice with its bounds.
Sections of the code: assumptions, definitions, theorems
Divide the code into logical sections following its own structure: the main body in execution order and each function at
the point where it is called. A section is one idea; it can be one line or several. If a single line needs small
subsections to be defined properly, make the subsections. A line coverage list at the start assigns every line of the
code that matters for the output (function headers, loops, returns, constant flags) to exactly one section; no line is
skipped. Every line of the code is proved: it is defined, its assumptions are stated, and a theorem says what it
establishes.


--- Page 36 ---
AutoAssumption: Searching over Assumptions Discovers ML-Systems Algorithms
Each section consists only of:
1. Assumptions. What the section needs to be true, continuing the numbering. Each assumption is a formal
statement with quantifiers written out, in method−independent terms (no line numbers, no document−internal
symbols, no forward references), so it can be compared with other methods’ assumptions. When a section reuses an
earlier assumption, restate it in one line with its label. A benchmark setting that fixes a flag or excludes a branch of
the code is an assumption here. An assumption the paper makes about a step and that the code relies on, as
described under the heading on building the proof on the benchmarked code, is an assumption here too, in the
document’s own words.
2. Definitions. One definition per object the section computes, as a formula, with every choice the code makes
spelled out (order, tie−break, boundaries, rounding). Each definition carries, inside it, the part of the code it
transcribes, so that the correspondence from code to mathematics is itself part of the record. Where the code
computes a thing in a particular way, the definition is the code’s way, and a lemma states what it equals.
3. Lemmas and theorems, with proofs. From the section’s definitions and assumptions: well−definedness, counts,
ranges, partition facts, and always a specification clause: what the section does to the property the specification is
about (preserves it, establishes it, or changes it by how much).
Every logic line of the code is a definition
Each line of the code that does something for the design’s purpose is stated explicitly as a definition (or as an
assumption, when it is a setting). Administrative lines, those that initialise components, register callbacks, log, reset
counters or move data between devices, are not stated; everything else is, down to initial values, shapes, boundary
cases, reductions and the exact form of the output.
A code coverage list names every function, branch and non−trivial statement of the code with the definition,
assumption or theorem that states it, and for the administrative lines the word administrative. Nothing is too small.
Each entry names the part of the code, the document object, and one of: defined, assumed (the setting that excludes
or fixes it), or administrative (cannot affect the output). An entry that could affect the output and has no definition is a
gap in the proof and must be closed before the document is finished.
Run the coverage test. When the document is drafted, and again after any change to it, go through the code line by
line and check that every line is proved somewhere: each line of the code maps to a definition, an assumption or a
theorem of the document, or is marked administrative with a reason. Check it in both directions: every entry of the
coverage lists points to an existing statement, and every logic line of the code appears in an entry. The test passes
only when no line is left uncovered; a single uncovered line means the proof does not describe the code, and the
document is not finished.
The purpose is that every design decision in the code is explicit in the document, that every concept introduced in the
code is covered by the mathematical notation, and that the covered pieces connect: each definition feeds the next,
and the main theorem is reached by chaining them.
The main theorem: the code meets its specification
Combine the section theorems into the claim of the problem statement. The proof of the main theorem is pointers to
the section theorems only. State explicitly every condition the claim needs (for strictness, for the output to be well
defined) and where each comes from (assumption or lemma).
Index of assumptions
At the end: number, title, where stated (problem statement or section name), short form. By section name, never by
line number.
Rules on sources
−Build mainly on the benchmarked code. Every definition is a transcription of a statement of the code. Use the paper
and the authors’ original code to understand the code, not to write the document.
−No quotations from the paper. Nothing from the paper’s text, formulas or numbers appears in the document. The
paper is read for motivation and for assumptions: when it states or implies an assumption behind a step the code
performs, that assumption is written as an assumption in the document’s own words, at the section that needs it, and
used like any other assumption. Every definition and theorem is derived from the code and the assumptions alone.


--- Page 37 ---
AutoAssumption: Searching over Assumptions Discovers ML-Systems Algorithms
Workflow for one design
1. Confirm the code is the version that ran. Read it fully. Read the matching parts of the original code and the method
section of the paper only as far as needed to understand it.
2. Divide the code into sections, as described under the heading on sections of the code, and list its logic lines for the
coverage lists.
3. Write the proof document in the order given above: only assumptions, definitions, lemmas, theorems, proofs.
4. Re−check the code. Read it again from top to bottom, with the finished document next to it, and confirm that every
definition, assumption and theorem describes the code exactly: same branches, same indexing, same rounding,
same ties, same boundary cases, every logic line with a definition and nothing in a definition that the code does not
do. Walk the code coverage list entry by entry against the code. Fix the document where they differ.
5. Run the coverage test: every line of the code must be proved somewhere in the document. The document is
finished only when it passes with no uncovered line.
6. Write the provenance record, as described under the heading on inputs and outputs.
7. Verification. Once everything is done, submit the proof document and its coverage lists to verification to catch any
errors. Fix every error it reports and submit again; repeat until no errors remain, at most 5 rounds. Report any error
still open after the fifth round.
Checklist
−The code is the version that ran: its hash matches the version that produced the results.
−Every line of the code is covered by the proof: the coverage test passes with no uncovered line.
−Every definition transcribes the code exactly, not the paper: same branches, indexing, rounding, ties and boundary
cases.
−The proof answers the problem: the main theorem proves the specification of the problem statement.
−Every condition the main theorem needs is a stated assumption or a proved lemma; nothing is assumed silently.


--- Page 38 ---
AutoAssumption: Searching over Assumptions Discovers ML-Systems Algorithms
D.2
Designing Lean from proof files
Prompt 2: writing the Lean proof from a proof document
How to write the Lean proof of a design from its proof document
The Lean proof formalizes a finished proof document. It shows that the design as implemented meets its specification
. Its main theorem is a statement about the document’s definitions, and the document’s definitions are transcriptions
of the benchmarked code, so the theorem is a statement about the code.
Inputs and outputs
Inputs:
−the finished proof document of the design, whose coverage test passes with no uncovered line;
−the benchmarked code the document was written against, with its hash.
Outputs, stored with the proof document:
−the Lean file;
−the provenance record of the proof document, extended with the hash of the Lean file.
Before writing any Lean
Re−check the code against the document. Read the code again from top to bottom, with the document next to it, and
confirm that every definition, assumption and theorem describes the code exactly: same branches, same indexing,
same rounding, same ties, same boundary cases, every logic line with a definition and nothing in a definition that the
code does not do. Walk the list that assigns every line of the code to a statement, entry by entry, against the code. If
they differ, fix the document first and run its coverage test again. Lean is only started once the document and the
code match.
The Lean file follows the document
The Lean file follows the document’s proof structure as closely as possible:
−one namespace per design, and a comment naming each document section, in document order;
−the problem’s assumptions are the fields of a structure; later assumptions are fields of further structures introduced
at the section that needs them, with the same labels in their docstrings;
−every definition of the document is a definition with the document’s label in its docstring; every section theorem is a
theorem with the same name and statement, including its specification clause; counts are their own lemmas;
−the main theorem is the statement of the document’s main theorem, proved from the section theorems in the same
order as the document;
−the main theorem depends only on Lean’s standard foundations (propext, Quot.sound, Classical.choice); no sorry
placeholder anywhere;
−indexing: say at the top which convention the Lean file uses and how document positions map to it.
The Lean file proves the same statement as the document, with the same intermediate lemmas in the same order.
Why the chain matters
A reader who trusts the Lean proof must be able to trust the code, because every object of the Lean file is a definition
of the document, and every definition of the document is a transcription of a named part of the code. If that chain
breaks anywhere (a definition that paraphrases the paper rather than the code, a logic line of the code with no
definition), the Lean proof does not say anything about the code, and the document must not claim that it does.
Workflow
1. Confirm the document’s coverage test passes and re−check the code against the document, as described under
the heading on what to do before writing any Lean.
2. Write the Lean file following the document, as described under the heading on how the Lean file follows the
document.
3. Compile it. Check what the main theorem depends on: only Lean’s standard foundations, no sorry placeholder.
4. Add the hash of the Lean file to the provenance record.


--- Page 39 ---
AutoAssumption: Searching over Assumptions Discovers ML-Systems Algorithms
5. Verification. Once everything is done, submit the Lean file to verification to catch any errors. Fix every error it
reports and submit again; repeat until no errors remain, at most 5 rounds. Report any error still open after the fifth
round.
Checklist
−The Lean file covers the code and the original proof document: every definition and theorem of the document is in it,
under the same label.
−Lean compiles with no errors, internal errors included; no sorry placeholder.


--- Page 40 ---
AutoAssumption: Searching over Assumptions Discovers ML-Systems Algorithms
D.3
Designing variants
Prompt 3: deriving a variant by changing one assumption
How to write a variant proof: perturb the assumptions of a design, derive a new design, prove its specification
A variant proof starts from a finished design proof (the parent) and produces the design proof of a new design (the
child). The child’s proof is the parent’s proof rewritten:
−every unchanged statement is copied verbatim;
−every change is marked so that a reader can tell what was removed and what was added, with the new text written
right after the old text it replaces;
−everything taken from another method is also marked as borrowed, with its source named.
The claim proved is the same: running the child’s code meets the parent’s specification. Always use the parent’s
problem definition: the child’s problem statement is the parent’s, copied verbatim.
Always start from the parent’s code and proof document. Before anything else:
1. Create a new workspace for the child, named after the parent and the variant.
2. Copy the parent’s code and proof document into it unchanged.
3. Make every change on these copies. The originals stay untouched: they give the parent’s hash, the impact set and
the final diff.
The principle: new designs come from perturbing assumptions
The parent’s proof makes every assumption of the design explicit. That list is the parent’s assumption set. Ideally, a
new design is made by changing that set and deriving the algorithm it calls for:
1. Relax an assumption: weaken it, widen its bound, or drop it.
2. Augment the system: strengthen an assumption, narrow its bound, or add a new one.
3. Re−derive. Work out which definitions no longer follow from the assumptions, which new definitions the changed
assumption requires or allows, and what the code must do differently. That code is the new design.
The direction is from assumptions to code, never from code to assumptions. A code tweak that changes no
assumption is not a variant in this sense. If an idea starts from the code, first find the assumption it perturbs. If the
parent’s proof does not state that assumption (because the design choice is built into a definition), write it as an
assumption first, then perturb it.
The best source of perturbations: what other methods assume
Methods for the same problem answer the same design questions differently. The answers are the assumptions of
their proofs. They are already collected in the assumption catalog that comes with the design proofs: every
assumption of every design proof, grouped by the question it answers (its class), with each method’s pseudocode.
Reuse this catalog; do not collect the assumptions again. Look through it for design features to reuse: an assumption,
a definition, a rule, a pseudocode line.
State every borrowing. If the child uses an assumption or design feature of another method, name the source (
method and label) in the perturbation summary and at the statement itself, and mark the borrowed text as borrowed
in the child’s proof.
To create a new design:
1. Pick a class in which the parent’s choice differs from what other methods assume.
2. Replace the parent’s assumption by another method’s variant, or by a combination of the two (both, a mixture, an
interpolation).
3. Derive the new design from the changed assumption set.
A technique that works in one method is then tried inside another design whose other assumptions stay fixed. This is
how ideas move between methods in a controlled way: one assumption at a time.


--- Page 41 ---
AutoAssumption: Searching over Assumptions Discovers ML-Systems Algorithms
Before borrowing, check the interface: the borrowed assumption must make sense with the parent’s other
assumptions (same objects, comparable units). If it does not, the derivation needs a compatibility step, marked as a
change: a change of units, a renormalisation, or an extra assumption.
Kinds of perturbation
The moves below are examples, not a complete list. You can also use a perturbation that fits none of them, or a
design feature that no other method has, if it is reasonable for the parent’s design. It still has to change an
assumption and be a good variant in the sense below. Such a feature is the child’s own, so mark it as a change, not
as borrowed.
−Borrow: replace the parent’s variant of a class by another method’s variant.
−Combine: keep the parent’s variant and add another method’s.
−Relax a bound: widen a range, or move to its endpoint.
−Augment a bound: narrow a range, or impose a floor.
−Drop: remove an assumption the code relies on.
−Add: a new requirement the design must satisfy.
−Split: a constant with two roles becomes two assumptions; perturb one.
−De−uniformise: one constant for all components becomes one per component.
−Change a quantifier: ”for all” becomes ”for a subset”; one aggregation becomes another.
−Interpolate: a parameter moving between two methods’ variants of one class.
Controls (random choices, inverted decisions) are not new designs. They are reference points and make effect sizes
interpretable.
What makes a good variant
1. One perturbation. One assumption is relaxed, augmented or borrowed, and every other edit follows from it. Two
independent perturbations make two new designs. Compose them afterwards if both are interesting.
2. The change is real. The perturbed assumption changes what the code executes in the benchmark. The child is not
equivalent to the parent: prove a separation lemma, a concrete input on which the two outputs differ. Before
spending GPU time, measure how often the two outputs differ on a few inputs.
3. The parent is a special case. Prefer a family with a parameter that has a value which recovers the parent. Prove a
reduction lemma: the child at that parameter value equals the parent. The lemma doubles as the check of the
implementation, and sweeping the parameter gives a dose−response curve.
4. Small proof delta. A small perturbation touches one or two sections of the proof. If changes spread everywhere,
the new design is far from the parent and no longer isolates one assumption.
5. Hypothesis from the proof, before the run. State what guarantee the perturbation removes or adds, and what that
predicts.
6. Let the proof reveal confounds. Compute the impact set first. It shows when one assumption plays two roles, or
when a perturbation silently triggers another theorem.
7. All else equal. Same hyperparameters, harness, samples, settings and models as the parent. Report the change
against the parent per setting, not only the mean.
8. Not a duplicate. The same (parent, perturbation) pair has not been built already. The finished child is not one−to−
one an existing method; otherwise it reuses that method’s code and is not new, so it is not a variant.
Marking changes
−Mark every change so that a reader can tell what was removed, what was added and what was borrowed, and
name the source of anything borrowed.
−Unchanged statements are verbatim: no rewording.
−Granularity: change the smallest unit (one bound, one symbol, one table cell, one pseudocode line, one code line).
If more than half of a statement changes, mark the whole statement as removed and restate it.
−A removed statement stays in place, marked as removed.
−Assumption labels stay the parent’s. A replaced assumption keeps the same number, with the old text marked as
removed and the new text added. A changed bound keeps the same number, with only the bound edited. A removed
assumption’s number is retired, never reused. An added assumption gets a suffix label (for example a letter after the
number) and is placed where first needed. Never renumber.
−An assumption, definition or pseudocode line taken from another method is new text and is also marked as


--- Page 42 ---
AutoAssumption: Searching over Assumptions Discovers ML-Systems Algorithms
borrowed, with its source (method and label) named first. A borrowed assumption keeps the child’s label. Its title also
names the class it comes from. Its symbols are rewritten in the parent’s notation.
The document, in order
1. Title: from the parent to the child, naming the changed assumptions, the changed lines of the code, and the proof
that the child meets the specification. Then a short note that tells the reader how removed, added and borrowed text
is marked.
2. Perturbation summary (facts only): the parent proof and its hash; the perturbed assumption, old and new, with its
class, and, if it is borrowed, the method and label it comes from; the code lines changed and the hash of the child’s
code; the impact set; the guarantees lost and gained.
3. Symbols and problem statement: the problem statement is the parent’s, verbatim; edits in the symbols only where
the perturbation reaches them.
4. Pseudocode, checked against the child’s code: a changed line is marked as removed, then the replacement
follows as an unnumbered added line; an added line is tagged with the previous number and a letter; a removed line
is marked as removed and keeps its number. The parent’s line numbers stay valid.
5. The code change: the touched lines of the code in file order, each marked as removed or added, ending with ”All
other lines are unchanged”. Then the list that assigns every line of the code to a statement and the list that assigns
every statement to the code it covers, with the changed entries marked.
6. Sections, in the parent’s order. For each statement, the treatment depends on its status. Outside the impact set:
copied verbatim. Hypothesis list changes: edit the list and re−check the proof. Conclusion changes: edit the
conclusion and the changed proof steps, and re−prove in full. Guarantee lost: mark the clause as removed and add a
weaker version with its extra hypothesis, if one holds. Guarantee gained: add a new lemma or theorem. Every
section theorem keeps its specification clause. If the child computes new quantities, extend the assumptions that
cover the parent’s quantities to cover them.
7. Main theorem for the child, then a short section ”the child versus the parent”: the reduction lemma; the separation
lemma; the proof delta list: every parent statement, by label and title, with its status.
8. Index of assumptions: changed, removed and added entries marked as such.
The impact set
Before editing, compute on the parent’s clean proof document, for the perturbed assumption (and, if needed, a
symbol it introduces):
1. the statements that cite the perturbed assumption (rewrite candidates);
2. the statements downstream of them (re−check what they use);
3. the statements that name it only inside a hypothesis range;
4. the table and index lines that mention it.
Only these statements can change. Everything else is copied verbatim. The list is a reading aid, not a proof: the final
re−read against the child’s code is still required.
Workflow
1. Pick the parent. List its assumption set, adding the implicit design choices as assumptions.
2. Open the assumption catalog. For each class, compare the parent’s choice with the other methods’ variants.
Choose one perturbation: borrow, combine, relax, augment, drop or add, or one of your own.
3. Create the child’s workspace and copy the parent’s code and proof document into it. All later steps edit these
copies.
4. Write the perturbed assumption, the hypothesis and the expected guarantees lost or gained, before any code.
Name the source method and label of anything borrowed.
5. Derive the new definitions. Implement them in the copied code with the smallest diff to the parent’s. Record the
hash and the diff.
6. Duplicate check, once the design is finished. Compare the child’s assumptions and pseudocode with every known
method. Look hardest at the method it borrows from and at the parent’s family. There must be no one−to−one match.
If one method could be identical, compare its outputs with the child’s on a few inputs. Identical outputs mean the
child is that method, not a variant: change the perturbation.
7. Before the GPU: the reduction check (the child at the parameter value that recovers the parent reproduces the
parent’s output) and the non−equivalence check (the outputs differ).
8. Compute the impact set on the parent’s original proof document. Apply the edits to the copied document in


--- Page 43 ---
AutoAssumption: Searching over Assumptions Discovers ML-Systems Algorithms
document order, marking each as removed, added or borrowed.
9. Re−read the child’s code top to bottom against the finished document.
10. Diff the child’s document against the parent’s: every difference must be a marked change (removed, added or
borrowed).
11. Run on the parent’s evaluation setting. Report the change against the parent per setting.
12. Literature review, once the design is finished. Search published papers, preprints and open−source code for
methods with the same assumptions or the same algorithm. List the closest ones with citations and say how the child
differs from each. If a published method matches the child one−to−one, the design is not novel: change the
perturbation.
13. Verification. Once everything is done, submit the child’s code, proof document and literature review to verification
to catch any errors. Fix every error it reports and submit again; repeat until no errors remain, at most 5 rounds.
Report any error still open after the fifth round.
Checklist
−Child workspace created; started from copies of the parent’s code and proof document.
−One assumption relaxed, augmented or borrowed; every other edit follows from it.
−Everything borrowed from another method: source method and label named, text marked as borrowed, interface
checked.
−The finished child checked against every known method: no one−to−one match.
−The perturbation changes what the code executes; separation lemma proved.
−Reduction lemma, if the child is a family.
−Impact set computed; everything outside it verbatim, everything inside it re−checked.
−Removed text and added text marked as such; assumption labels stable.
−Specification clauses re−confirmed; main theorem proved for the child.
−Guarantees lost and gained listed; hypothesis written before the run.

E
OPENEVOLVE AND AIDE AS RUN HERE
OpenEvolve (Sharma, 2025), an open implementation of AlphaEvolve (Novikov et al., 2025), evolves a population of
programs in a MAP-Elites archive; AIDE (Jiang et al., 2025) is a tree search over whole programs that drafts, improves or
debugs one node per step. Both run unmodified from pinned releases (OpenEvolve v0.4.0, commit 162c3fe; AIDE v0.2.2,
commit ad73d22), start from the same parent code as our harness, and use the same model (Claude Fable 5.1, high effort,
through an OpenAI-compatible proxy), the same two-stage evaluator (CPU checks on tiny random models, then the 12
protocol cells on the GPU queue) and the same budget: ten GPU-evaluated algorithms or 25 model calls.
Shared settings.
Settings not listed below are the release defaults. Both tools call Claude Fable 5.1 (effort high) with
no temperature, a reply cap of 100,000 tokens and a 3,600 s call timeout, and give the evaluator a 36,000 s timeout, since
one evaluation waits for 12 queued GPU jobs. Each search stops at ten GPU-evaluated algorithms or 25 model calls, and
we repeat it with three seeds per parent. None of these changes tunes a tool for a better score; each adapts it to the shared
protocol.
OpenEvolve.
OpenEvolve runs diff-based evolution with evolve blocks enforced (enforce evolve blocks =
true), so edits outside the evolve block are reverted, which closes a reward hack that CacheCraft reports (Poudel et al.,
2026). We shrink the population to fit ten algorithms: one island with a population of 20 and an archive of 10, no migration
(migration rate = 0), and five MAP-Elites feature bins, since the default five islands of 1,000 programs would never
fill in ten algorithms. The elite, exploration and exploitation ratios are 0.2, 0.2 and 0.7; the prompt shows the three top
programs and no diverse programs.
OpenEvolve evaluates
the algorithms
one at a
time,
so
each algorithm
sees all
earlier ones.
With
parallel evaluations = 1 and a single cascade threshold of 0.5, algorithm k sees algorithms 1, . . . , k −1 and
their per-cell score tables, which needs an artifact limit of 40,960 bytes. The code-length limit is 80,000 characters, since the
parents have 400–650 lines.
AIDE.
AIDE starts from the parent, with Fable as the coding model for drafting, improving and debugging. We insert the
parent as the root node with its measured score (num drafts = 1) instead of five drafts from scratch, so AIDE starts
where the other searches start. Code formatting is off, so the parent’s file is not rewritten, and every program runs in our
two-stage evaluator instead of AIDE’s interpreter.
AIDE takes its metric only from our evaluator. There is no review or report model: the evaluator’s score is the metric,
so no model call can report a metric that was not measured, and the metric is maximised (metric maximize =
true) rather than inferred. The step limit is 25 with the same stop at ten GPU-evaluated algorithms; debug prob and
max debug depth keep their defaults of 0.5 and 3.
