ALL ALGORITHMS
We formalized 89 algorithms, each with one proof graph: 44 for KV-cache eviction, 26 for speculative decoding and 19 for
LLM weight pruning. The count is of proof graphs. It includes published configurations that combine or modify published
methods (such as CaM on top of TOVA or LAMP on top of Wanda) and four standard baselines: autoregressive decoding,
speculative sampling in two draft-length settings and the dense model. It leaves out the two reference points of KV-cache
eviction, no compression and random eviction. The 44 KV-cache eviction algorithms are 30 KVPress algorithms, among
them H2O (Zhang et al., 2023), SnapKV (Li et al., 2024a), PyramidKV (Cai et al., 2025), KNorm (Devoto et al., 2024),
CaM (Zhang et al., 2024b), AdaKV (Feng et al., 2025), Expected Attention (Devoto et al., 2025), KeyDiff (Park et al.,
2025), CUR (Sengupta et al., 2025) and CAP (Yang et al., 2026), and 14 ported algorithms, among them EchoPress (Lin
et al., 2026) and DefensiveKV (Feng et al., 2026). The 26 speculative-decoding algorithms are 5 Spec-Bench algorithms
(Lookahead (Fu et al., 2024), PLD (Saxena, 2023), REST (He et al., 2024), SAM-Decoding (Hu et al., 2025b) and token
recycling (Luo et al., 2025)), 18 ported implementations and 3 baselines.
The 19 LLM weight-pruning algorithms are the dense model and 18 published algorithms and published settings (such
as DSnoT without skipping, RIA with channel permutation and LAMP on top of Wanda or SparseGPT), among them
magnitude pruning (Han et al., 2015), LAMP (Lee et al., 2021), SparseGPT (Frantar & Alistarh, 2023), Wanda (Sun et al.,
2024), OWL (Yin et al., 2024), DSnoT (Zhang et al., 2024c), E-Sparse (Li et al., 2023), GBLM-Pruner (Das et al., 2023),
RIA (Zhang et al., 2024a), Pruner-Zero (Dong et al., 2024), ALPS (Meng et al., 2024) and Z-Pruner (Bhuiyan et al., 2025).
Figure 4 draws three algorithms of each field.

G
UNCERTAINTY ESTIMATION
The error bars of the paper come from three sources of variation, and each figure uses the one that varies between its runs. A
KV-cache eviction score is deterministic for a given set of questions (greedy decoding, fixed seed), so its uncertainty comes
from which questions were drawn. A speculative-decoding speedup is a ratio of wall-clock times, so its uncertainty comes
from repeating the same runs. A search result depends on the search’s own random choices and on the model’s replies, so its
uncertainty comes from repeating the search. Unless stated otherwise, ± and error bars are one standard deviation (SD), and
tests are two-sided, made cell by cell at p < 0.05 and not corrected for the number of cells.
G.1
KV-cache eviction: resampling the questions
The SD of a KV-cache eviction score comes from a bootstrap over its questions. A RULER score is the mean over the 13
tasks of the per-task accuracy on the drawn questions (LongBench: 16 tasks). We resample the questions of each task with
replacement, keeping each task’s count, recompute the score, and repeat this 10,000 times; the SD of the 10,000 scores is
the bootstrap SD reported next to every score. It says how much the score would move under another draw of the same
number of questions, and it shrinks with that number: 0.2 to 0.5 points per cell at 6,500 RULER-4K questions.
Means over cells and differences between two algorithms combine the per-cell SDs. A mean over cells (the 12 model–factor
cells, the two models, or the six factors) treats the cells as independent runs, so the SD of a mean of k cells is
qP
i sd2
i /k.
A difference between two algorithms has SD
q
sd2
a + sd2
b and we test it with a z-test; this ignores that both algorithms
answer the same questions, which usually makes the test conservative. The mutation study pairs the two instead: it scores
the mutant and its parent on the same resampled questions, and the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the 10,000 resampled
differences give a 95% interval.
G.2
Speculative decoding and systems profiles: repeating the runs
Each Spec-Bench cell runs three times with seed 0, and its error bar is the SD over these runs. We submit run k of the parent
and run k of the variant back to back to the same machine, and each speedup divides by the autoregressive run of the same
model and temperature. A cell reports the mean of the three runs and, as its error bar, their sample SD; we test a difference
with a paired t-test over the three run pairs (two degrees of freedom). This SD measures timing variation (clock speeds,
scheduling, other jobs on the machine), not variation over questions: every run uses the same 480 questions. Accepted
tokens per target pass (#MAT) are identical in every run at a fixed seed, so they carry no error bar and their differences are
exact.
The systems profiles measure variation over questions instead, with a paired bootstrap. The profiles behind panels G and I of
Figure 7 run three paired timing runs per cell on all 480 Spec-Bench questions; the error bars of panel G are the SD over the
three runs, those of panel I the SD of a paired question bootstrap (10,000 resamples of the question ids, the same resample
applied to every run and to the paired autoregressive passes). Table 8 and the panel C of Figure 7 use seven passes over two
fixed prompts; their error bars are the sample SD over the passes.
G.3
Design searches: repeating the search
Each harness runs three times from the same parent. OpenEvolve and AIDE take a different seed in each repeat. Our harness
has no seed: the repeat number only labels the run, and the model’s proposals are not seeded, so its repeats largely replay the
same sequence of moves. Figure 8 plots, after each algorithm, the mean over the three repeats of the running-best score,
with error bars spanning the minimum and maximum over the repeats; the text also reports the sample SD over the repeats.
The min–max range and the SD are rough estimates, and both understate the variation of our harness. Both contain
the search’s own variation and the question-draw uncertainty of each score (about 0.45 points for a 12-cell mean at 200
questions). With three repeats, each is itself a rough estimate, and for our harness, whose repeats are not independent, each
understates the variation one would see across independent searches.

H
THE WORKED EXAMPLE IN FULL
Section 2.1 sketched why speculative sampling (Leviathan et al., 2023) is exact; this appendix walks through the whole
argument. A small drafter proposes tokens, the large target model checks them in one pass, and the text that comes out must
be distributed exactly as if the target had written it alone. We first fix the setting and the problem, then follow one drafted
token through the accept-or-resample step, show that the token that comes out has the target’s law, extend this to a block of
drafts and to the whole loop, and end with how many tokens one target pass buys.
Every statement carries the name it has in Figure 3, whose graph is repeated below; that figure shows Assumption A5,
Definition D3, Theorem T1 and the problem P word for word. Every lemma, theorem and the corollary below is proved in
Lean 4 with Mathlib, statement for statement (no sorry, no added unproved statement).

Figure 3. The proof graph of this appendix, repeated from Figure 3. Lines are drawn after transitive reduction, so indirect citations are
omitted; the arrows into P come from the claims that answer the problem. Enlarged discs mark Assumption A5, which SVIP relaxes, and
the exactness and token-count claims; the dark curve along the bottom is the only citation of Assumption A5, by Theorem T2.
In the repeated graph (Figure 3), each disc is the statement of the same name below; a line from one disc to another means
the second cites the first.
H.1
The setting and the problem
Two language models share a finite vocabulary V. We write V∗for the finite sequences over it, u ∈V∗for a prefix, and call
a map V →[0, 1] that sums to 1 a distribution on V. The first assumption says what the large model is: something that,
given a prefix, returns a distribution over the next token. Where it matters, an assumption also says what it does not require,
because that is what the agent is allowed to change.
Assumption A1 (Target distribution over a finite vocabulary). For every prefix u ∈V∗the target model Mp defines
a distribution p(· | u) on V. Temperature, top-k and nucleus adjustments are folded into p (standardized sampling);
temperature 0 makes p(· | u) a point mass on an arg max (ties broken by a fixed rule). Nothing is assumed about how p
depends on u.
The second model is the drafter. It must use the same vocabulary, and nothing else is asked of it: the argument has to work
however poor the drafter is.
Assumption A2 (Draft distribution over the same vocabulary). For every prefix u the draft model Mq defines a distribution
q(· | u) on the same V as Assumption A1. Nothing relates q to p: q need not be close to p, need not have q(x | u) > 0
where p(x | u) > 0, and may be a point mass.
With the two models fixed, the problem can be stated.
The problem P.
Given a target model Mp and a cheaper drafter Mq over the same vocabulary, emit a continuation whose
law is exactly that of autoregressive sampling from Mp (Corollary C1), while one target call emits up to γ + 1 tokens, with
the expected number given by Theorem T2.


--- Page 48 ---
AutoAssumption: Searching over Assumptions Discovers ML-Systems Algorithms
H.2
One position: accept or resample
Speculative sampling decides the fate of one drafted token at a time. Fix one position and write p, q for the target’s and the
drafter’s distributions there. A token is accepted with certainty when the target likes it at least as much as the drafter, and
otherwise only in proportion:
Definition D1 (Acceptance probability). For p and q at one position (Assumptions A1 and A2), a(x) = min
␀1, p(x)/q(x)

when q(x) > 0, and a(x) = 1 when q(x) = 0. (The value at q(x) = 0 never matters: such an x is never drawn from q. A
Lean file is free to use its own convention for division by zero; Lemma L1 holds for every choice.)
A rejected token is not replaced by a fresh draw from p, which would give the accepted tokens too much weight. The
replacement comes from the part of p that acceptance leaves uncovered:
Definition D2 (Residual distribution). For p and q at one position (Assumptions A1 and A2) let Z = P
x max(0, p(x) −
q(x)). If p̸ = q then Z > 0 (if Z = 0 then p ≤q everywhere, and as both sum to 1, p = q), and p′(x) = max(0, p(x) −
q(x))

Z. For p = q set p′ = p; by Lemma L3 the branch that draws from p′ then has probability 0, so any distribution
would do.
The step also needs its randomness to behave: drafts drawn from q, an acceptance coin drawn independently of them, and a
replacement drawn from the residual. The assumption is stated for a step of γ drafts, used later; a single position is its first
draft.
Assumption A3 (Independent verifier randomness). Within a step at prefix u the random draws are the draft tokens
x1, . . . , xγ, the verifier’s r1, . . . , rγ and one final token x′ (the residual token after a rejection, otherwise the token appended
after a full acceptance). (i) Given everything drawn before it, xi has law q(· | u x1:i−1) of Assumption A2. (ii) Each ri is
uniform on [0, 1] and independent of (x1:γ, r1:γ \ ri). (iii) The residual token, given everything drawn before it, has the
residual distribution of Definition D2 for the position at which it is drawn. (iv) The draws of a step are independent of the
draws of earlier steps given the prefix at which the step starts.
Together these make one step:
Definition D3 (One speculative-sampling step at one position). Draw x ∼q (Assumption A2) and r ∼U[0, 1] (Assump-
tion A3). If r ≤a(x) (Definition D1) the step accepts and emits x; otherwise it rejects and emits x′ ∼p′ (Definition D2).
Two pointwise identities carry all the algebra that follows. The first says that a token is drafted and then accepted with
probability min(p, q); the second that the residual weight of a token is what p has left beyond that minimum.
Lemma L1 (Pointwise identities). For every x ∈V, with a of Definition D1: (a) q(x) a(x) = min(p(x), q(x)); (b)
max(0, p(x) −q(x)) = p(x) −min(p(x), q(x)).
Proof. (a) If q(x) = 0 both sides are 0, since p(x) ≥0. If q(x) > 0 and p(x) ≥q(x) then a(x) = 1 and both sides are
q(x). If q(x) > 0 and p(x) < q(x) then a(x) = p(x)/q(x) and both sides are p(x). (b) If p(x) ≥q(x) both sides are
p(x) −q(x); otherwise both are 0.
How often does a step accept? Leviathan et al. (2023) name this rate and relate it to a divergence between the two models:
Definition D4 (Acceptance rate and divergence, Defs. 3.1 and 3.2 of Leviathan et al. (2023)). β = Pr(accept) in
Definition D3, and DLK(p, q) = P
x|p(x) −M(x)| with M = 1
2(p + q).
Summing the first identity over all tokens gives the rate in closed form, and the second identity shows that the residual is
normalized by exactly the probability of a rejection:
Lemma L2 (Acceptance rate, normalizer, divergence; Lemma 3.3 and Theorem 3.5 of Leviathan et al. (2023)). Under
Assumption A3, the acceptance rate β and the divergence DLK of Definition D4 and the normalizer Z of Definition D2
satisfy β = P
x min(p(x), q(x)), Z = 1 −β, and DLK(p, q) = 1 −β.
Proof. By Assumption A3(ii), r is independent of x and uniform, so Pr(accept | x) = Pr(r ≤a(x)) = a(x) because
a(x) ∈[0, 1]; hence β = P
x q(x) a(x) = P

Finally, a step can only be sure to accept when the two models agree, which is the case that Definition D2 set aside:
Lemma L3 (When nothing is rejected). 0 ≤β ≤1, and β = 1 if and only if p = q.
Proof. By Lemma L2, β = P
x min(p(x), q(x)); 0 ≤min(p, q) ≤p pointwise and P
x p(x) = 1, so 0 ≤β ≤1. If β = 1
then P

H.3
The emitted token has the target’s law
Everything is now in place for the central claim: whatever the drafter, the token that one step emits is distributed as p. The
proof adds up the two ways a token can come out, accepted as a draft or drawn from the residual.
Theorem T1 (Exactness of one step; Leviathan et al. (2023)). Under Assumptions A1–A3, the token emitted by Definition D3
has law p: Pr(emit y) = p(y) for every y ∈V.
Proof. The step emits y either by accepting a draft equal to y or by rejecting and drawing y from p′; the two events are
disjoint, so
Pr(emit y) = Pr(accept, x = y) + Pr(reject, residual = y).
Accept path. Pr(accept, x = y) = q(y) Pr(r ≤a(y) | x = y) = q(y) a(y) = min(p(y), q(y)), by Assumption A3(ii) and
Lemma L1(a). Reject path. By Assumption A3(iii) the residual token, given (x, r), has law p′, so Pr(reject, residual =
y) = Pr(reject) p′(y) = (1 −β) p′(y). Case p̸ = q. By Lemmas L2 and L3, Z = 1 −β > 0, so (1 −β) p′(y) =
max(0, p(y) −q(y)) = p(y) −min(p(y), q(y)) by Lemma L1(b), and the two paths add to p(y). Case p = q. By
Lemma L3, β = 1, the reject path has probability 0, and the accept path gives min(p(y), p(y)) = p(y).
One position is therefore exact. A real step, however, drafts several tokens before the target checks any of them.
H.4
From one token to a block, and to the whole loop
In the code the drafter writes γ tokens one after another, and the target then checks all of them in a single forward pass. The
next assumption says what that pass returns and how its verdicts are used.
Assumption A4 (Token-wise verification). At prefix u with drafts x1:γ, the target forward pass returns the γ+1 distributions
pi = p(· | u x1:i−1), i = 1, . . . , γ + 1, of Assumption A1; drafted token xi is verified against pi with draft distribution
qi = q(· | u x1:i−1) of Assumption A2; the first rejection ends the step; if all γ drafts are accepted, one token is drawn from
pγ+1, given everything drawn before it, and appended.
Exactness is a claim about whole sequences, so we name the law that the target alone gives a sequence,
Definition D5 (Autoregressive reference). For a prefix u and L ≥0, P AR
L
(y1:L | u) = QL
t=1 p(yt | u y1:t−1) with p of
Assumption A1, the law of L tokens sampled one at a time from Mp.
and the step exactly as the code runs it:
Definition D6 (A step of γ tokens, as the code runs it). At prefix u: draw x1, . . . , xγ in order, xi ∼q(· | u x1:i−1)
(Assumption A2; the drafter’s autoregressive loop); obtain p1, . . . , pγ+1 from one target pass (Assumption A4); draw
r1, . . . , rγ (Assumption A3); let n = min{ i : ri > ai(xi) } −1, with n = γ if there is no such i, where ai is Definition D1
for (pi, qi). The step emits the block y = x1:n x′, where x′ ∼p′
n+1 (Definition D2 for pn+1 against qn+1) if n < γ and
x′ ∼pγ+1 if n = γ. The block has n + 1 ∈{1, . . . , γ + 1} tokens.
Because all γ drafts are drawn before any of them is verified, it is not obvious that the emitted tokens still behave as fresh
steps of Definition D3. The next lemma shows that they do; it is the only place where the order of the draws matters.
Lemma L4 (Token-level kernel of a step). Consider Definition D6 at prefix u under Assumptions A1–A4. Let 1 ≤i ≤γ,
let y1:i−1 ∈Vi−1, and let Ei = {n ≥i −1, x1:i−1 = y1:i−1} be the event that the first i −1 drafts equal y1:i−1 and were
all accepted. If Pr(Ei) > 0 then, conditional on Ei, the i-th emitted token yi has law p(· | u y1:i−1). For every y1:γ with
Pr(n = γ, x1:γ = y1:γ) > 0, conditional on this event the (γ + 1)-th emitted token has law p(· | u y1:γ).

Proof. Ei is determined by (x1:i−1, r1:i−1). By Assumption A3(i), conditional on x1:i−1 = y1:i−1 the draft xi has law
q(· | u y1:i−1), and conditioning further on r1:i−1 does not change this, since by (ii) the r’s are independent of the
drafts; by (ii) again, ri is uniform and independent of (xi, x1:i−1, r1:i−1). So conditional on Ei the pair (xi, ri) has law
q(· | u y1:i−1) ⊗U[0, 1]. By Assumption A4, pi = p(· | u y1:i−1) and qi = q(· | u y1:i−1) on Ei. On Ei the step is
still running at position i, and the i-th emitted token is xi if ri ≤ai(xi) and the residual draw of position i otherwise,
which by (iii) has law p′
i given everything before it. This is exactly Definition D3 for (pi, qi), so Theorem T1 gives the
law pi = p(· | u y1:i−1). The last claim is Assumption A4: given everything drawn before it, the appended token has law
pγ+1 = p(· | u y1:γ).
Repeating the block step gives the loop,
Definition D7 (The speculative loop). Starting from u, repeat Definition D6 at the current prefix and append the block, until
at least L tokens have been emitted; P SpS
L
(· | u) is the law of the first L emitted tokens Y1:L.
and the loop is exact: its first L tokens have the law of L tokens sampled from the target one at a time.
Corollary C1 (Exactness of the loop). Under Assumptions A1–A4, P SpS

Proof. Let Y1, Y2, . . . be the emitted tokens of Definition D7 in order. We show that for every 1 ≤t ≤L and every y1:t−1
with Pr(Y1:t−1 = y1:t−1) > 0,
Pr(Yt = y | Y1:t−1 = y1:t−1) = p(y | u y1:t−1)
for every y ∈V;
(1)
the chain rule then gives Pr(Y1:L = y1:L) = QL
t=1 p(yt | u y1:t−1) = P AR
L
(y1:L | u).
Token t is emitted by some step; which step, and at which position i ∈{1, . . . , γ + 1} within it, is determined by the
lengths of the blocks emitted before it. Let H = (ℓ1, . . . , ℓk) range over the lengths of the blocks that end before token t
(ℓ1 + · · · + ℓk ≤t −1, the next block containing token t); the events {Y1:t−1 = y1:t−1} ∩H partition {Y1:t−1 = y1:t−1},
so it suffices to prove (1) conditional on each such cell of positive probability. Fix H; it places token t at position
i = t −(ℓ1 + · · · + ℓk) of a step that started at prefix w = u y1:t−i, and on the cell the first i −1 tokens of this step
are yt−i+1:t−1 and were accepted. By Assumption A3(iv), the draws of this step are independent of the earlier steps
given w, so conditioning on the earlier steps (which fix w and H up to this step) changes nothing about this step beyond
fixing w. If i ≤γ the cell is the event Ei of Lemma L4 for the step at w with y1:i−1 := yt−i+1:t−1, so Yt has law
p(· | w yt−i+1:t−1) = p(· | u y1:t−1). If i = γ + 1 the cell says n = γ with x1:γ = yt−γ:t−1, and the last claim of
Lemma L4 gives the same law. Hence (1) holds on every cell, and therefore on their union.
The proof applies to the idealized loop defined above, with its stated conditional sampling and independence assumptions. It
does not certify arbitrary stopping rules or the measured SVIP cap branch.
H.5
How many tokens one target pass buys
Exactness says nothing about speed. The speedup comes from emitting more than one token per target pass, and to count
them Leviathan et al. (2023) idealize the acceptances:
Assumption A5 (Fixed draft length, independent acceptances). γ ≥1 is a constant, and in a step of Definition D6 the first
i drafts are all accepted with probability αi (0 ≤i ≤γ) for a rate α ∈[0, 1], as when acceptances are independent with
common rate α, e.g. when β of Definition D4 equals α at every prefix. This is an idealization used only by the cost claim
(Theorem T2); the exactness claims never cite it.
Under this idealization the count is a geometric sum.
Theorem T2 (Expected tokens per target pass; Equation (1) of Leviathan et al. (2023)). Under Assumption A5, a step of
Definition D6 emits E[n + 1] = Pγ
i=0 αi tokens, which is (1 −αγ+1)/(1 −α) for α < 1 and γ + 1 for α = 1.
Proof. n + 1 = Pγ
i=0 1[the first i drafts are accepted], since the indicator is 1 exactly for i ≤n. Under Assumption A5 the
i-th indicator has expectation αi; sum the geometric series.

Without Assumption A5, for a fixed maximum draft length the general tail-sum identity is E[n+1] = Pγ
i=0 Pr(A1∩· · ·∩Ai),
with the empty intersection (i = 0) having probability one. Here Ai denotes acceptance at position i. Prefix-dependent
rates cannot in general be multiplied as unconditional marginal probabilities; adaptive draft lengths additionally require
accounting for whether a position was proposed.

I
MUTATION STUDY
I.1
Exactness proofs of published decoders
Formalizing a field also checks the algorithms already in it. We prove exactness for eight published speculative decoders
under stated cache, tie-breaking and exact-arithmetic assumptions; five of them claimed it without proof (Gante, 2023;
Mamou et al., 2024b; Zhang et al., 2025; Agrawal et al., 2024).

Benchmark score
Figure 14. Lean flags every mutant; the benchmark
flags about half. An evaluation is one design at one
setting, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct or Qwen3-8B at 16× or
64× compression, so each design counts four times.
Lean gives one verdict per design, shared by its four
settings; the benchmark flags any score below the par-
ent’s, the rule most favourable to it. Blue cells are correct
decisions and red cells wrong ones, shaded by their share
of the row.
We took five verified KV-cache eviction algorithms (KNorm, SnapKV,
KVGrad, RestoreKV and KVzip) and wrote 14 code mutants. Each
mutant injects one realistic bug, such as keeping one pair too many or
too few, reversing a ranking, skipping a layer or forgetting to protect
the sink tokens; comment-only edits and an equivalent rewrite serve as
five controls. We checked each parent’s fixed Lean proof against the
mutated code and ran every mutant and control on 200 RULER-4K
questions. Every mutant breaks its proof and every control passes, yet
in 26 of the 56 mutated evaluations the score matches or exceeds the
parent’s: some bugs are too small to move the score, and others raise
it by silently exceeding the memory budget, such as keeping every
pair.
